# Related Work

This paper investigates whether electrophysiological plant signals carry
information about human emotional states, how those states are labeled by
Facial Emotion Recognition (FER) and Heart Rate Variability (HRV), and
whether ambient CO~2~ concentration, recorded alongside, could account for
any such relationship. This chapter reviews the relevant background in four
areas: plant bioelectricity and human–plant interaction, the theoretical
structure of human emotions, automated emotion recognition via FER, and
HRV as a scale for emotional arousal. It closes by identifying the
resulting research gap.

## Human Emotion Classification based on Plant Bioelectrical Signals

The most important foundation for this study is the pilot investigation
about human emotion classification based on plant bioelectrical signals
[@gloor2025]. Gloor examines whether bioelectrical signals from a single
plant could be used to classify environmental conditions (light on/off)
and human emotions. Using an AD8232 ECG sensor, mel-spectrograms, and a
ResNet18 CNN, lamp detection was achieved with an accuracy of
85.4-85.9%. For emotion classification, it is distinguished between
happy and sad based on automated FER labels, resulting in an accuracy of
72.8-73.8%. In addition, different time delays between emotional
expression and the plant signal are used. The optimal time delay is
identified as one second. Gloor [@gloor2025] used a vehicle acting as a Faraday
cage as well as aluminum foil acting as dummy electrodes for control
experiments to reduce (but not completely eliminate) the possibility of
trivial electromagnetic artifacts. The study explicitly emphasizes the
preliminary, exploratory nature of the findings and the need for further
replication [@gloor2025].

## The Circumplex Model

Both the categorization of emotions into positive and negative valence
classes used by Gloor [@gloor2025] and the IAPS/SAM methodology
developed by Choi et al. [@choi2017] are based on the influential
circumplex model presented by Russell [@russell1980]. Using four
methodologically independent scaling procedures, Russell [@russell1980]
shows that affective states can consistently be
represented as a two-dimensional, bipolar space along the axes of
valence (pleasure-displeasure) and arousal (arousal-sleep). This model
provides the theoretical justification for grouping heterogeneous
emotion categories (e.g., "happy/surprise" vs. "fear/anger/sad/disgust")
into higher-order valence classes.

![The two-dimensional circumplex structure of affect, spanned by a valence and an arousal axis, following Russell [@russell1980]. Emotion words within one quadrant agree in the sign of both axes and differ mainly in intensity. Figure reproduced from Lee et al. [@lee2025].](figures/circumplex_model.png){#fig-circumplex width=80%}

@fig-circumplex shows this space. The two axes divide it into four
quadrants, each collecting emotion words that agree in the sign of both
valence and arousal: *excited*, *delighted*, and *happy* differ in
intensity but all combine positive valence with high arousal, and the
same holds for the remaining three quadrants. It is this quadrant, rather
than the individual emotion word, that the present study treats as the
classification target. A recorded window therefore counts as emotionally
classified when the classifier places it in one of the four quadrants —
high-arousal positive (I), high-arousal negative (II), low-arousal
negative (III), or low-arousal positive (IV), referred to below as
*positive activated*, *negative activated*, *negative calm*, and
*positive calm*. Windows that stay near the neutral centre of either axis
carry no directional information and are assigned the neutral class
instead. @sec-labeling-algorithm describes the rule that implements this
crossing.

## Automated Emotion Recognition Using HSEmotion

Savchenko [@savchenko2022] presents HSEmotion, an open-source library
for FER. It is based on EfficientNet architectures and is optimized for
speed and mobile use. The models were first trained on a face
identification task (VGGFace2 dataset) and then fine-tuned on images from
AffectNet to classify emotions. HSEmotion achieved accuracies ranging
from approximately 55-70% and inference times of 59-191 ms on mobile
devices. These figures illustrate that even highly developed FER systems
perform significantly below perfect classification accuracy and may
contain systematic, data-set-dependent bias. This is of central
importance for the evaluation of automatically generated emotion labels,
such as those used in this study, since false classifications of the FER
component directly influence the validity of every subsequent analysis
that relates those labels to physiological or bioelectrical signals.

## Heart Rate Variability as Emotional Scale

HRV is frequently used to supplement or validate subjective measures of
emotion. Choi et al. [@choi2017] evaluated the validity of HRV to label human emotions
with 30 participants. Five photos were selected for each of the
categories of "happy," "unhappy," and "neutral" from among the images
provided by the International Affective Picture System (IAPS)
[@choi2017]. The extracted R-R interval (RRI) value is compared to the
valence, arousal, and dominance value from the self-assessment. The
results show a significant correlation between RRI and the subjective
ratings of valence and dominance only for the category of unpleasant and
highly arousing stimuli. In contrast, no significant correlations are
found for neutral and pleasant stimuli. The authors conclude that HRV
can serve as a valid measure of emotion, but only when emotional arousal
is high enough. This finding is relevant to the research question of
this study, because it suggests that the correlation between plant
signals and HRV data may also be modulated by arousal and is not
expected to be linear across all emotion categories.

## Research Gap

Taken together, the reviewed work shows that plant bioelectrical signals
can be classified into coarse human-emotion categories [@gloor2025], yet
this evidence stems from a single-subject, exploratory design without a
standardized elicitation protocol. The circumplex model [@russell1980]
and the documented validity limits of FER [@savchenko2022] and HRV
[@choi2017] further suggest that a binary happy/sad framing is too coarse
to reveal where plant signals actually carry emotional information. It
therefore remains open whether the association replicates across
multiple participants under a controlled stimulus, and whether it holds
separately for valence and arousal. The present study addresses this
gap.
